title: Kestrel and the Room
premise: Urban explorer Wendell Voss has spent a decade documenting the Kestrel Building's unmapped sub-basements, dismissing the voices in her sleep recordings as equipment artifacts. When the recordings reveal a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, she discovers the tunnels are a holding place for something taken from a family in 1974 — a child's remains and the confession buried with them. As the entity binds itself to her, Wendell must trace the surviving perpetrators of that year's crime and return what was stolen before the building finishes claiming her as its new keeper. In the end, she gives the truth to the last living victim, unseals the room at terrible personal cost, and walks out changed — belonging now to neither the world above nor below.
about_author: R. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent years cataloguing condemned properties in the industrial Midwest. Their fiction draws on real survey discrepancies and the quiet violence hidden in property records.

chapters.title: The Survey Gap
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She maps a tunnel beneath the Kestrel Building that appears on no city survey, noting fresh airflow where there should be none. The chapter establishes her decade-long obsession and her habit of rationalizing anomalies. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity curdling into the first admission that she may have wanted to find this.

chapters.title: Questions Answered
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Reviewing her sleep-recorder audio, she hears a second voice — dry, patient — answering questions in her own cadence. She cross-references dates with tunnel visits and realizes it responds to what she does, not what she says. Emotional beat: denial collapsing into dread; she stops sleeping alone in her apartment.

chapters.title: What the Deed Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, intercut with 1974 documents. At the county archive she finds the Kestrel family trust, a sealed probate file, and a missing-person report for Ada Kestrel, age nine, filed and withdrawn within a week. Emotional beat: the thrill of research giving way to horror as she recognizes the withdrawal signature belongs to the man who still owns the building.

chapters.title: Descent Protocol
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She returns to the tunnels wired for light and sound and finds a room that wasn't there in any prior visit: wallpapered, furnished like 1974, a child's belongings arranged neatly. The voice speaks her name. Emotional beat: awe weaponized into terror; she flees but leaves behind her recorder, which the room keeps.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Terms
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The entity begins appearing in reflections and dreams, showing her fragments of 1974: three men, a locked cellar, a decision made to protect reputations. It names its terms — return what was taken, or become the next thing that waits. Emotional beat: bargaining; she tries to negotiate rules and learns the room has no interest in fairness.

chapters.title: Two Survivors
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Wendell and Harold Finch, one of the three men, now dying in a care home. Wendell confronts him; he confesses in pieces, insisting they meant to move Ada and never did. His terror confirms the room is real and that he's been paying since 1974. Emotional beat: the sickening weight of complicity; justice and cruelty blur.

chapters.title: Everything Wendell Kept
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The room escalates, taking things she loves — her archive of ten years of exploration vanishes, then memories begin going. Her sister Mara arrives worried after a disturbing phone call and becomes an anchor and a liability. Emotional beat: grief and isolation; Wendell understands the room isolates keepers first.

chapters.title: Harold Goes Home
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wendell brings the dying Harold to the Kestrel Building, believing his confession delivered on-site will satisfy the terms. The room accepts his words but not his life, taking him anyway — and shows Wendell that confession without restitution is just another theft. Emotional beat: horror at her own miscalculation; the plan was never enough.

chapters.title: Ada
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, deep beneath the building. She uncovers Ada's remains and the truth: the men didn't lose her, they buried her to bury their crime. Wendell carries her out through collapsing tunnels while the room screams its claim on her. Emotional beat: fierce, sacrificial resolve; she chooses the living over her obsession.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, weeks later. Ada is buried under her own name; the Kestrel heirs finally know; the building stands silent and its tunnels appear on the new survey, ordinary at last. But Wendell still hears the voice faintly in every recording — patient, waiting for the next keeper. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; justice done, and a debt that never fully closes.
